title: Learning How to Doubt. Part 4
scripture_text: ‘’After Jesus had finished instructing his twelve disciples, he went on from there to teach and preach in the towns of Galilee. When John, who was in prison, heard about the deeds of the Messiah, he sent his disciples to ask him, “Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect someone else?” Jesus replied, “Go back and report to John what you hear and see. The blind receive sight, the lame walk, those who have leprosy are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, and the good news is proclaimed to the poor. Blessed is anyone who does not stumble on account of me.” As John’s disciples were leaving, Jesus began to speak to the crowd about John: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed swayed by the wind? If not, what did you go out to see? A man dressed in fine clothes? No, those who wear fine clothes are in kings’ palaces. Then what did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet. This is the one about whom it is written: “I will send my messenger ahead of you, who will prepare your way before you. Truly I tell you, among those born of women there has not risen anyone greater than John the Baptist; yet whoever is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he. From the days of John the Baptist until now, the kingdom of heaven has been subjected to violence, and violent people have been raiding it. For all the Prophets and the Law prophesied until John. And if you are willing to accept it, he is the Elijah who was to come. Whoever has ears, let them hear.’’
devotional:
How did John express his doubt?

There are a number of lessons we can learn from how John went about expressing his doubt.

He was vulnerable enough to share his doubt with others.

It is very tempting for people who are in a position of leadership to feel that they need to be strong, that they are to protect those for whom they are responsible, from knowing their weaknesses or insecurities, so they feel the need to have all right answers, and always feel in control. But John was not like that. He did not feel a need to protect his reputation, he was prepared to share his fears and doubts.

He needed help to share his doubts with Jesus.

John was restricted, shut up in prison, he needed help. Doubt may be one of the things God uses to deepen our communication with Him, but this does not mean that we will not need the help of others. These disciples of John listen to what he had to say, and then went to Jesus on his behalf. When a person shares their doubts with us, we need to do all we can to help them through their doubt. Being faithfully committed to a doubting person is very important.

How did Jesus respond to John’s doubt?

Three things Jesus did not do

He did not condemn John but commended him. It was in the context of John expressing his doubt that Jesus said “I tell you the truth: Among those born of women there has not risen anyone greater than John the Baptist.” There is a lot of discussion about this verse, but I think that it’s significant that Jesus says these words in this context. When we are totally honest with Jesus, then our hearts are more open to receive his encouragement and comfort. Jesus will always defend those who have honest doubts. The interesting thing about these words in this context is that Jesus cared for John enough to defend John’s reputation.

Jesus did not change Johns circumstances. John was in prison, John stayed in prison, John was murdered in prison. If anything, his circumstances got worse. As we have been saying, the roots of doubt are never external, of course when a persons goes through great suffering, it can inflame their doubt, and if life had been made a little bit easier for John it may have helped medicate the pain of his doubt. But what Jesus wanted to do was much bigger than change John’s circumstances, he wanted to assure him that everything was going according to plan, (although maybe not Johns plan!)

Jesus did not change anything he was doing in order to accommodate John’s doubts.

When a person is full of insecurity, with feelings of vulnerability and confusion because of painful doubt, it is very easy for them to lash out at others, blaming them hoping that they change. Jesus understood that he did not need to change; what he was doing was consistent with His Father’s will. Doubting people can become angry and demanding. When John asked his question, he was challenging Jesus, attempting to force his hand, to press Jesus to announce that He was the Messiah, and to cause Him to begin to bring judgement to the earth. John had warned men that the Messiah would come with fire, and John may have thought it was high time for Jesus to get on with it.
prayer: Father may I be like John and have the humility, wisdom and courage to express my doubts.
